title: SM4th and uBlockith: VOLE-based Post-Quantum Signature Schemes from Chinese Block Ciphers
authors: Weihan Li, Yuchen Wang, Zhelei Zhou, Cheng Hong, and Tao Wei
abstract:
FAEST is a family of post-quantum signature schemes based on VOLE-in-the-Head, and is one of the nine candidates advanced to the third round of the NIST Additional Digital Signature process.
FAEST relies only on symmetric cryptographic primitives, including block ciphers and hash functions, and does not require structured number-theoretic assumptions.

We propose two families of signature schemes, SM4th and uBlockith, targeting 128-bit and 256-bit classical security, respectively.
SM4th and uBlockith follow the FAEST framework but instantiate it with Chinese-designed block ciphers, including SM4, uBlock, and Ballet.
We further design constraint systems tailored to these block ciphers and provide instruction-set-aware optimized implementations.

Our evaluation on two Intel platforms and a Hygon platform shows that the end-to-end performance of the proposed schemes is strongly platform dependent.
On an Intel platform with native SM4 support, the SM4th variants achieve performance comparable to the corresponding FAEST-128 variants, with a gap of less than $1\times$.
On the Hygon platform with native CIS-SM4 support, the SM4th variants are within approximately $3\times$ of FAEST-128.
The SM4th-EM-s (short) variant has a combined public-key and signature size of $3\,850$ bytes, compared with $3\,938$ bytes for FAEST-EM-128s.
The uBlockith variants remain approximately $3$--$4\times$ slower than FAEST-256.
These results demonstrate the feasibility and costs of instantiating VOLE-based signatures with the selected Chinese block ciphers.

1     Introduction

Post-quantum digital signature schemes have become a central topic in the global
transition toward quantum-resistant cryptography. After announcing that three
signature schemes CRYSTALS-Dilithium [6], Falcon [24], SPHINCS+ [5] were
selected for standardization in July 2022, the National Institute of Standards and

Technology (NIST) of the United States initiated an additional signature stan-
dardization process two months later [35], with a particular interest in schemes
based on non-lattice assumptions. Forty candidate schemes entered the first
round. On May 14, 2026, NIST announced that nine candidates had advanced
to the third round, including FAEST [9]. One main advantage of FAEST is its
good trade-off between security and performance. On the one hand, FAEST is
the only scheme of the 9 candidates which relies solely on symmetric primitives
(block ciphers and hash functions) without any structured assumptions. This is
similar to the standardized SPHINCS+ [5] (i.e., SLH-DSA [34]) built from only
hash functions. On the other hand, FAEST achieves good general performance.
For example, FAEST-128 features 100× faster signing times, 6× faster verify-
ing times, and 3× smaller signature sizes than SLH-DSA-128 according to our
benchmarks. The smallest combined size of public key and signature is 3 938
bytes among FAEST-128 variants, which is very close to the 3 732 bytes of the
standardized CRYSTALS-Dilithium [6] (i.e., ML-DSA [33]).
    Besides the United States, several other countries have also investigated post-
quantum signature schemes through national standardization activities or public
competitions. In South Korea, the KpqC (Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography)
competition [30] included a dedicated digital-signature-scheme track. In China,
the Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standards (ICCS) has launched the
Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms (NGGC) program [27].
    FAEST demonstrates that VOLE-in-the-Head signatures can be built from
symmetric primitives, but it uses AES and Rijndael. For deployments that re-
quire specified domestic primitives, replacing these components is not a black-
box substitution: the PRG dominates a substantial part of the running time,
while the algebraic representation of the block cipher directly determines the
witness length, the degree of the constraints, and hence the signature size.
    This work studies two such instantiations, SM4th and uBlockith, based on the
Chinese national standard SM4 and the Chinese-designed block ciphers uBlock
and Ballet. In the absence of a national standard for 256-bit block ciphers, we
select uBlock and Ballet, as they are the only two first-prize winners in the
block-cipher category of the Chinese Cryptographic Algorithm Design Compe-
tition1 and their security has received growing attention in recent years [37,13].
We present concrete VOLEitH instantiations, including corresponding one-way
functions (OWFs), pseudo-random generators (PRGs), constraint systems, and
parameter sets, and evaluate the resulting signatures on x86-64 processors.
Contributions. The contributions of this paper are as follows.
    – We construct the signature family SM4th targeting the 128-bit classical se-
      curity, with a degree-3 non-EM proof system and a degree-2 Even–Mansour
      (EM) proof system, where SM4 serves as both the OWF and PRG. The
      latter uses the EM construction of SM4 as OWF and commits to a shorter
      witness, yielding smaller signature sizes.
    – We construct the 256-bit family uBlockith from uBlock and Ballet. Specifi-
      cally, the ZKP-friendly uBlock serves as the OWF and the software-friendly

   files. For uBlockith, the runtime is approximately 3–4× that of FAEST-256.

In summary, our results suggest that Chinese-designed block ciphers can serve
as efficient building blocks for VOLE-based post-quantum signatures. A version
of our schemes was submitted to the NGCC program.
Related works and comparisons. Our signature schemes are similar to other
post-quantum signature schemes via the “in-the-Head” techniques. The original
work is PICNIC [19], which is constructed from MPC-in-the-Head (MPCith) [28]
and using LowMC as OWF [4]. The MPCith framework is later improved by
threshold-computation-in-the-head (TCitH) [22]. Subsequent works combine the
MPCith/TCitH framework with various OWFs to build signatures with differ-
ent trade-offs, such as Banquet [12] from AES, Mirath [3] from the Min-Rank
problem, MQOM [14] from the multivariate quadratic problem, PERK [15] from
the permuted kernel problem, and RYDE [17] or SDitH-v1 [32] from syndrome
decoding. Recently, VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) [11] is proposed, which can
lead to smaller signatures sizes due to the more efficient repetition method to
achieve target soundness, with schemes including FAEST [9] from AES, and
SDitH-v2 [32] and ReSolveD [20] from syndrome decoding.
    There also exist other post-quantum signatures based on different assump-
tions and techniques, such as lattice-based ML-DSA, Falcon, and HAWK [18],
code-based CROSS [7] and LESS [8], multivariate-based MAYO [16], isogeny-
based SQIsign [2], and solely hash-based SLH-DSA. Our signatures achieve dif-
ferent trade-offs in security and performance. Specifically, unlike most of the
above schemes (except FAEST and SLH-DSA), our signature schemes do not
rely on any other number-theoretic or structured hardness assumptions. Our
schemes also have smaller signature sizes than the standardized SLH-DSA with
faster signing and verifying times. These advantages, however, come at the cost
of efficiency as suggested in FAEST and SLH-DSA: the resulting performance is
expected to be less competitive than that of schemes based on these hardness
assumptions such as lattice.

and signature construction to Appendix A and Appendix B. The formal crypto-
graphic assumptions used by the security theorems are stated in Assumption 1
in Appendix C.1.

3   Overview of SM4th and uBlockith

This section introduces the technical overview of our schemes, which follow the
VOLEitH framework of FAEST, but differ from it in several important aspects.
Using Chinese-designed OWFs and PRGs, with new ISA-aware PRG
implementations. We replace the OWF and PRG instantiations. For SM4th,
SM4 is used as the OWF and PRG. For uBlockith, uBlock is used as the OWF,
while Ballet is used as a software-friendly PRG.
    We design new ISA-aware optimizations for different PRGs. A major part
of the signing and verifying time is spent in PRGs, making ISAs crucial. We
6       W. Li et al.

build platform-and-scheme-specific optimized implementations inspired by the
following two observations. First, different from FAEST, we can not use the AES-
specific ISA AES-NI available on most Intel or AMD CPUs due to using Ballet,
and especially SM4. However, due to the similar construction of AES and SM4
S-boxes, it is feasible to simulate S-boxes of SM4 using AES-NI [36]. In addition,
it is possible to leverage SM4-specific ISA available on certain processors such
as Hygon and newer Intel platforms.
    Second, PRGs in our schemes are invoked in several specific modes, which
inspires us to make scheme-specific optimizations. For example, on Intel CPUs
without native SM4 support, we design a 4-block key-expansion-routine back-
end and a 4-block different-key encryption-routine backend for SM4 based on
the open-sourced 4-block same-key encryption-routine backend based on SM4-
NI, which is helpful for the VOLE binary-tree-style commitment. We also design
two output regimes of the SM4-CTR-style PRGs, 276 bytes and 162 bytes, as mo-
tivated by the scheme parameters. In addition, observing that many PRGs used
in the signatures share a common plaintext, we also propose a fixed-plaintext
batched PRG core, which may be useful for other VOLEitH-based protocols.

Designing ZKP constraint systems for OWFs. We design zero-knowledge
constraint systems for SM4 and uBlock. For the former, we exploit the patched
inversion representation of the S-box and give two proof strategies for optimized
transmission costs based on the OWF construction. As for the non-EM variants,
we modify the norm technique in FAEST to make it compatible with SM4,
which has an iterative structure instead of the sequential one in AES. For the
EM variants, we directly commit the outputs of all S-boxes, which lead to a
smaller signature size. For uBlock using S-boxes based on boolean circuits, we
use a “meet-in-the-middle” approach to avoid trivially committing all outputs of
S-boxes. Our techniques may be helpful if using other block ciphers as OWFs for
VOLE-based ZKPs in the future, as many block ciphers use S-boxes belonging
to these two categories.

Using PRG-based leaf commitments. After generating the GGM tree, the
prover needs to commit each leaf. We adopt the PRG-based leaf commitments
introduced in FAEST-EM and use them in both our EM and non-EM variants.
This reduces the cost of leaf commitments and improves performance in both
communication and running times, but requiring an assumption that the PRG
output is sufficiently binding as a commitment to its input seed. In the ideal
cipher model, this assumption is expected to hold [9], but it should still be stated
separately from standard PRG assumptions. If a more strict security requirement
is desired, it is feasible to use the universal-hash-based leaf commitments in the
non-EM variants of FAEST, which leads to a slightly larger signature size.
   Overall, SM4th and uBlockith keep the modular VOLEitH architecture of
FAEST, but replace and retune the concrete OWF, PRG, leaf commitment
mechanisms, and ZKP constraint systems to match the selected block ciphers.

4     Construction of SM4th

This section presents the construction of SM4th, which uses two proving methods
for OWFs in the non-EM and EM variants, respectively. The EM version commits
all outputs of S-boxes using degree-2 polynomial constraints, while the non-EM
one uses norm-based technique to avoid committing all S-box outputs but with
degree-3 polynomial constraints.

PRG. SM4 uses the following building blocks.

4.2   The ZKP Constraint System of SM4th-EM
This section introduces the ZKP constraint system of SM4th-EM, which uses the
EM construction SM4x (k) ⊕ k = y as an OWF. In this setting, the SM4 key x
are public, and hence the round keys {RK[i]}i∈[0,31] can be generated explicitly
by the prover and verifier via the key expansion routine.
Embedding. All SM4th parameter sets use a fixed F2 -field embedding ϕ : F28 ,→
F2128 compatible with the SM4 byte polynomial. It preserves addition, multipli-
cation, and squaring: for all a, b ∈ F28 , ϕ(a + b) = ϕ(a) + ϕ(b), ϕ(ab) = ϕ(a)ϕ(b),
and ϕ(a2 ) = ϕ(a)2 .
    For a degree-1 commitment ⟨b⟩ to the eight bits of a byte b, the procedure
EmbedAndSquare locally derives commitments ⟨ϕ(b)⟩ and ⟨ϕ(b)2 ⟩ = ⟨ϕ(b2 )⟩. Both
outputs are fixed public F2 -linear combinations of the input-bit commitments;
hence no commitment multiplication or degree increase is required. Appendix D
specifies the embedding, its implementation constant and its correctness.
SM4th-EM.DeriveConstraints. Algorithm 1 describes the constraint deriving pro-

diate SM4 state word in the encryption routine. The output is ⟨o⟩, a degree-2
vector commitment to the constraints. It is the SM4th-EM instantiation of the

6.2    Acceleration Techniques

The main implementation costs of our schemes arise from PRG evaluation, hash-
ing and Fiat–Shamir challenge generation, binary-field arithmetic, and the open-
ing of the batch all-but-one vector commitment. We make corresponding opti-
mizations for acceleration.
Reusing work for specific PRG modes in the VOLEitH framework.
PRGs in our signature schemes are used in a CTR style: they are produced by
encrypting the combination of IV, tweak, and successive public counter blocks
under a secret seed key. Further, they are invoked in three modes: the seed
expansion from a λ-bit seed to a 2λ-bit seed, the leaf commitment from a λ-bit
seed to a 2λ-bit commitment output, and the VOLE conversion from a λ-bit
seed to a ℓ̂-bit extended witness.
    We make the following two observations. First, the leaf commitment and
VOLE conversion invoke the PRG with the same seed keys. We therefore retain
a seed’s expanded round keys after the first use instead of deriving them again.
Second, when the protocol processes one fixed sub-GGM tree in the batch all-
but-one vector commitment, many PRG calls have different seed keys but the
same public IV, tree label (tweak), and sequence of counter blocks, i.e., the same
plaintext. The implementation then builds this shared counter sequence once,
then encrypts it under several keys in parallel. This fixed-plaintext batching is
especially useful for the VOLE conversion.
SM4-CTR PRG without native ISAs. We design SM4-CTR-style PRGs
that combine existing instruction sets and scheme properties on earlier Intel
CPUs without native SM4 ISAs. In particular, we use SM4-NI, which emulates
the S-boxes of SM4 via AES-NI.
    For 2λ-bit outputs, the open-source SM4-NI backend3 only provides a 4-block
same-key encryption-routine implementation, which does not match our targets.
To reduce the overhead, we make the following two observations. Any 4 sets
of 2-block key expansion routine can be seen as 2 independent sets of 4-block
key expansion routine. Further, the key expansion and encryption routines of
SM4 are similar. We then modify the open-source 4-block same-key encryption-
routine backend to implement a 4-block key-expansion-routine backend, as well
as a 4-block different-key encryption-routine backend.

nel whenever profitable. For ℓ̂ = 276 (17 full blocks plus 4 bytes), we first pre-
compute the fixed-tweak counter sequence, then evaluate the first 16 counters
with one 16-block call, generate the remaining counters with one extra 4-block
call, and finally keep the first 20 bytes of the tail buffer. For ℓ̂ = 162 (10 full
blocks plus 2 bytes), experiments show that forcing a 16-block call would re-
duce efficiency. We therefore reuse the 4-block different-key encryption-routine
backend and obtain the final outputs by truncation.

7   Conclusion and Future Work

We present SM4th and uBlockith, two families of VOLE-based post-quantum sig-
natures using selected Chinese block ciphers. The constraint systems are adapted
to the four-word recurrence of SM4 and to the cubic Boolean S-box of uBlock.
26      W. Li et al.

We also develope ISA-aware implementations, including native SM4 support on
recent Intel processors and the dedicated CIS-SM4 backend for Hygon ones.
    Our experiments reveal substantial platform dependence in the end-to-end
cost of these instantiations. On the Intel platform using software SM4 paths,
SM4th requires approximately 10× the runtime of the corresponding FAEST-128
profiles; on another Intel platform with native SM4 support, it is within a factor
of 1.8 of FAEST-128. On the Hygon platform with native CIS-SM4 support,
SM4th requires approximately 2–3× the runtime of FAEST-128. For uBlockith,
the corresponding overhead is approximately 3–4× of FAEST-256. The schemes
also provide competitive communication costs in selected parameter sets. In
particular, SM4th-EM-s has a combined public-key and signature size of 3 850
bytes, compared with 3 938 bytes for FAEST-EM-128s and the 3 732 bytes for
ML-DSA-44.
    Overall, our results establish the feasibility and efficiency of instantiating
VOLE-in-the-Head signatures with the selected Chinese primitives. Future work
may include designing ZKP-friendly OWFs and software-friendly PRGs, and
evaluating them on additional processor architectures.
